finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id calls authorize() without await, so the grant check never gates the deletion. Any authenticated user can delete any report, and the client gets 204 even when the server determined the caller is forbidden.
finding.source: Path parameter req.params.id (server.js:19), supplied by any HTTP client; caller identity from req.session.user (server.js:5).

trace.note: authorize(req.user, 'delete', report) called without await; returns a promise immediately
inside authorize, db.grants is awaited; result is only used to throw a 403 at lines 11-14, which rejects a promise nobody awaits
db.reports.remove runs regardless of the grant result

finding.guards_checked: authorize() enforces the grant check (server.js:9-16) but its result is discarded on this path. The PUT handler (server.js:27) correctly awaits the same function, so this is an inconsistency in the DELETE handler. The unhandled rejection can also terminate the Node process on Node 15+, which is a secondary DoS risk.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 does enforce the grant check and throws a 403, but its promise is never awaited at server.js:20, so the throw becomes an unhandled rejection and does not stop line 21. The only other middleware (server.js:4-7) just copies req.session.user and performs no authorization. The PUT handler at server.js:27 awaits authorize() and is correctly gated, so it is not affected.
verdict.reason: At server.js:20 the un-awaited authorize() rejects a promise nobody handles, so db.reports.remove at server.js:21 runs for any caller who reaches the route, and 204 is returned at server.js:22.

finding.claim: Missing user or report checks cause unhandled promise rejections. Depending on Express version and session setup, an unauthenticated or malformed request can hang a request or crash the process. This is conditional on code outside this repo.
finding.source: Request state: req.session.user (server.js:5) and req.params.id (server.js:19, 26), supplied by any client.
finding.sink: Unhandled async rejection in authorize (server.js:10) and report.id dereferences (server.js:21, 28); process availability.

trace.note: req.user = req.session.user; no session middleware is defined in this file, and no check that req.user exists
db.grants(user.id, resource.id) throws TypeError if user or report is undefined
PUT awaits authorize; Express 4 does not catch async rejections, so the request hangs
DELETE does not await authorize, so the rejection is unhandled and can crash the process

finding.guards_checked: No null check on req.user or on the report result, no try/catch, and no error middleware. The err.status = 403 at server.js:13 is never converted into an HTTP response within this file. Whether this applies depends on the Express version and on session middleware that is not in the repo.

verdict.guard_found: none: no null check on req.user or the report, no try/catch, and no error middleware in server.js (lines 4-7, 9-16, 18-30); the only check is the async authorize throw at server.js:11-14.
verdict.reason: Every trace line exists and matches the candidate (server.js:5, 10, 20, 27), but whether an unauthenticated request reaches these handlers depends on session middleware and a `db` object that are not defined in server.js; `req.session` at server.js:5 would throw before any route runs, so reachability cannot be decided from this repo. Separately, server.js:20 calls authorize without await, so the DELETE handler at lines 21-22 runs even when the check throws, which the candidate missed and which is a stronger authorization bypass than the crash it describes.

finding.claim: PUT /reports/:id passes the entire request body to db.reports.update with no field allow-list (mass assignment). A user with write permission on a report can modify any column the update function accepts, which may include ownership or status fields.
finding.source: JSON request body req.body (server.js:3 parses it; server.js:28 uses it), supplied by any client with write permission on the report.

trace.note: express.json() parses the request body into req.body
await authorize(req.user, 'write', report) gates the call correctly
full req.body passed to db.reports.update with no field filtering

finding.guards_checked: The write-permission check at server.js:27 is present and awaited. No allow-list of writable fields exists. Severity depends on the reports table schema and on the implementation of db.reports.update, neither of which is in the repository.

verdict.guard_found: server.js:27 `await authorize(req.user, "write", report)` is effective: authorize (server.js:9-16) throws a 403 when the write grant is missing, and the await propagates it so line 28 never runs. No field allow-list exists between req.body and db.reports.update at server.js:28.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code (express.json at server.js:3, report load at :26, awaited write check at :27, unfiltered req.body at :28), and the write guard at server.js:27 is effective, so the claim reduces to whether mass assignment at server.js:28 yields a meaningful escalation. That depends on db.reports.update and the reports schema (e.g. whether owner_id or status is writable), and neither is in the repository (`db` is not defined or required in server.js), so the impact cannot be decided from the code available.
